body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Physiotherapist-led exercise by video versus in person for knee osteoarthritis: a randomised non-inferiority comparison","authors":"Lindahl-Mwangi C, Okafor-Stein R, Brennan-Tran H","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice","doi":"10.5555/jmpp.2021.0318","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Background: exercise therapy is first-line care for knee osteoarthritis, but attendance at hospital classes is limited by travel. Methods: we randomly allocated 175 adults with knee osteoarthritis to six weeks of physiotherapist-led group exercise by video or the same programme in person, with a non-inferiority margin of 8 points on the KOOS pain subscale. Results: at 12 weeks the mean difference in KOOS pain change was 1.4 points in favour of in-person exercise (95 percent CI -2.9 to 5.7), within the margin. Session attendance was 78 percent by video and 81 percent in person. Satisfaction scores were similar. Participants were recruited from urban clinics and needed their own device. Conclusions: video delivery was non-inferior for pain at 12 weeks in people who could use the technology."},{"title":"Telehealth-delivered exercise therapy for knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised comparisons","authors":"Petrov-Achebe N, Sandoval-Reid J, Kamau-Lindgren T","year":2023,"venue":"Osteoarthritis Rehabilitation Reviews","doi":"10.5555/orr.2023.0052","providerType":"meta-analysis","abstract":"We searched five databases to June 2022 for randomised comparisons of exercise therapy delivered by telehealth for knee osteoarthritis. In total, 14 trials with 1,720 participants were included. Compared with in-person exercise, telehealth-delivered exercise showed no important difference in pain (standardised mean difference 0.05, 95 percent CI -0.10 to 0.20) or in physical function. Compared with no exercise, telehealth exercise improved pain and function. Heterogeneity was moderate. Most trials excluded people without internet access, and adults over 75 and people with low digital literacy were under-represented, which limits applicability to rural and older populations. Certainty was rated moderate for pain and low for function."},{"title":"Older adults' experiences of group exercise classes delivered by video: an interview study","authors":"Haddad-Olsen M, Fitzgerald-Nnaji E","year":2020,"venue":"Ageing and Rehabilitation Qualitative Studies","doi":"10.5555/arqs.2020.0147","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 19 adults aged 65 to 86 who had taken part in physiotherapy group exercise classes by video. Participants valued not having to travel or arrange transport and said they exercised more regularly at home. Frustration with technology was common in the first sessions, and several said a practice call before the first class would have helped. Some missed the social contact of an in-person class and found it harder to ask questions in a video group. Participants who lived alone relied on family members to set up the device. The authors recommend a technology check before the first session and small groups that allow questions."},{"title":"Attendance and completion in a rural telehealth knee exercise programme: a service cohort","authors":"Ferreira-Oyelaran L, McAllister-Dube K, Suzuki-Hale P","year":2024,"venue":"Rural Allied Health Reports","providerType":"cohort study","abstract":"We describe 212 people with knee osteoarthritis who started a six-week video exercise programme run by a rural hospital physiotherapy service. Overall, 71 percent completed the programme. Completion was 52 percent among participants without home broadband and 76 percent among those with it, and 60 percent among participants aged over 75 compared with 74 percent among younger participants. Among completers, the mean KOOS-12 summary score improved by 9.8 points at six weeks. Outcomes were not recorded for people who stopped attending, and there was no comparison group, so the improvement cannot be attributed to the programme alone."},{"title":"Reliability of the 30-second chair stand test performed by video call in people with knee osteoarthritis","authors":"Nakagawa-Brooks A, Olumide-Varga S","year":2019,"venue":"Physiotherapy Measurement Notes","doi":"10.5555/pmn.2019.0203","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared the 30-second chair stand test performed at home by video call with the same test performed in clinic on the same day in 48 people with knee osteoarthritis. Agreement was high (intraclass correlation 0.91), and the mean difference was 0.4 stands, with more stands counted in clinic. Two participants could not position the camera to show the whole movement, and one test was stopped because the chair was unstable. The authors recommend a standard chair height, a camera check and a second observer for the first remote test."},{"title":"Digital exclusion and exercise therapy: who declines video-based physiotherapy and why","authors":"Obi-Castellano R, Wainwright-Adeyemi J, Lund-Takahashi M","year":2022,"venue":"Health Services and Inclusion","providerType":"mixed methods study","abstract":"We invited 340 people referred for knee or hip exercise therapy to choose video-based or in-person physiotherapy and interviewed a purposive sample of those who declined video. Of the 340 people invited, 29 percent declined video-based physiotherapy. Declining was more common among people with limited English (46 percent) and among those without a smartphone. Interviews described fear of not coping with the technology, lack of a private space at home, and worry about being seen exercising by others in the group. Loaned devices and a telephone setup call were described as helpful by those who accepted after initially declining."},{"title":"Travel distance and attendance at hospital physiotherapy for knee osteoarthritis in a rural region","authors":"Grant-Mahlangu D, Eriksen-Obafemi T","year":2016,"venue":"Journal of Rural Musculoskeletal Care","doi":"10.5555/jrmc.2016.0077","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We examined attendance records of 406 patients with knee osteoarthritis referred to hospital physiotherapy in a rural region. The median one-way travel distance was 68 km. Attendance was 83 percent of booked sessions among patients living within 20 km and 61 percent among those living more than 60 km away. Patients without a car and those relying on community transport attended least. Distance was also associated with longer waits for a first appointment. The authors suggest that services for dispersed rural populations consider remote delivery for exercise-based care."}]}
